Name: Pool Model (Shared Everything)
Strategy: Single database and schema shared by all tenants with tenant_id column
Strengths: Lowest infrastructure cost; simplest operations; easy to add tenants
Weaknesses: Noisy neighbor risk; complex queries need WHERE tenant_id everywhere; compliance concerns for data residency
When to Use: SaaS with many small tenants; cost-sensitive; uniform workload patterns
Gotcha: Missing a WHERE tenant_id clause causes cross-tenant data leak — use row-level security policies

Name: Silo Model (Shared Nothing)
Strengths: Strongest isolation; independent scaling; simplest compliance; per-tenant backup/restore
Weaknesses: Highest cost; operational complexity scales with tenant count; onboarding is slow
When to Use: Enterprise tenants with strict compliance; high-value tenants with custom SLAs; regulated industries
Gotcha: Infrastructure-as-code is essential — you can't manually manage 500 tenant databases

Name: Bridge Model (Hybrid)
Strategy: Shared compute with per-tenant databases or schemas
Strengths: Good balance of isolation and cost; per-tenant data residency possible; simpler than full silo
Weaknesses: Schema migrations must run across all tenant databases; connection pool management is complex
When to Use: Mid-market SaaS with 50-500 tenants; varying compliance requirements per tenant
Gotcha: Schema drift between tenant databases is a silent killer — enforce migration idempotency

Name: Row-Level Security (RLS)
Strategy: Database-enforced policies that filter rows by tenant_id automatically
Strengths: Prevents accidental cross-tenant access at DB layer; transparent to application code
Weaknesses: Performance overhead on large tables; complex to debug; not all databases support it equally
When to Use: Pool model where defense-in-depth is required; PostgreSQL and SQL Server have mature RLS
Gotcha: RLS policies must be tested extensively — a misconfigured policy silently leaks data

Name: Noisy Neighbor Mitigation
Strategy: Rate limiting and resource quotas per tenant to prevent one tenant from degrading others
Strengths: Prevents cascading failures from tenant traffic spikes; fair resource sharing
Weaknesses: Requires per-tenant metrics and enforcement; adds latency for tracking; hard to set right limits
When to Use: Any shared-resource multi-tenant system; especially with variable workload patterns
Gotcha: Setting limits too tight loses customers; too loose defeats the purpose — use adaptive limits based on tenant tier

Name: Per-Tenant Rate Limiting
Strategy: Separate rate limit buckets per tenant with tier-based quotas
Strengths: Prevents abuse; enables tiered pricing; protects shared infrastructure
Weaknesses: Token bucket per tenant requires distributed state (Redis); adds latency per request
When to Use: Multi-tenant APIs with tiered pricing; platforms with API consumers
Gotcha: Rate limit keys must include tenant_id not just IP — multiple tenants may share IPs

Name: Tenant-Aware Caching
Strategy: Prefix cache keys with tenant_id; optional per-tenant cache size limits
Strengths: Prevents cache poisoning across tenants; enables per-tenant cache policies
Weaknesses: Increases key space; reduces cache hit rate vs global cache; memory overhead for small tenants
When to Use: Any cached multi-tenant system; especially when tenants have different data shapes
Gotcha: Cache invalidation must be tenant-scoped — a global flush for one tenant's change is wasteful

Name: Tenant Onboarding Automation
Strategy: Automated pipeline to provision all resources for a new tenant
Strengths: Fast time-to-value; consistent setup; reduces human error; enables self-service
Weaknesses: Complex to build initially; must handle partial failures during provisioning
When to Use: Any multi-tenant system beyond 10 tenants; especially silo and bridge models
Gotcha: Provisioning must be idempotent — retries on failure shouldn't create duplicate resources

Name: Tenant Data Export and Portability
Strategy: API or process to export all of a tenant's data in standard format
Strengths: Compliance requirement (GDPR portability); builds customer trust; enables migration
Weaknesses: Complex for systems with many data stores; must include related data across services
When to Use: Any B2B SaaS; required by GDPR for EU customers; enterprise sales requirement
Gotcha: Export must be complete and consistent — partial exports cause more problems than no export

Name: Schema-Per-Tenant
Strategy: Shared database server with separate schema (namespace) per tenant
Strengths: Better isolation than pool; easier compliance than pool; per-tenant schema evolution possible
Weaknesses: Schema migrations across hundreds of schemas is slow; connection pool per schema adds overhead
When to Use: Mid-size SaaS with 10-200 tenants; PostgreSQL schema support is excellent for this
Gotcha: PostgreSQL search_path must be set per-connection — connection pool configuration is critical

Name: Tenant-Aware Logging and Observability
Strategy: Include tenant_id in all logs and metrics; per-tenant dashboards
Strengths: Enables per-tenant debugging; tenant-specific SLO tracking; usage-based billing data
Weaknesses: Increases log volume; cardinality explosion in metrics with high tenant count
When to Use: Any multi-tenant system; essential for debugging tenant-specific issues
Gotcha: High-cardinality tenant_id labels can crash Prometheus — use recording rules or exemplars instead

Name: Cross-Tenant Analytics
Strategy: Aggregated analytics across all tenants for platform insights while maintaining isolation
Strengths: Platform-level insights; benchmark data for customers; product analytics
Weaknesses: Must ensure no PII leakage across tenants; aggregation must be pre-computed not ad-hoc
When to Use: Platform operators needing usage analytics; benchmark features for enterprise customers
Gotcha: Differential privacy or k-anonymity needed if sharing benchmarks — raw aggregates can leak tenant identity
